text_translated_detailed: having taken their lands again into the grace of the Dutch state, they marched on the 22nd of December with the aforementioned 500 white-clad, mostly well-trained soldiers, and approximately 4 to 500 inhabitants from the villages of Sinckan, Soulangh, and Baccaluan toward the village of Pagcareijang, where Formosa [Taiwan] was taken and completely burned with fire. After we had marched for a long time (having passed through many beautiful flat fields, small woods, and small rivers, as well as some large rivers), we arrived on the 25th of the same month around midday, and encountered some troops of theirs, who at first came very fiercely at our people and the front troop, but seeing some of theirs fall underfoot and be wounded, they began to retreat into the long reeds and some fled toward the village. Thereupon their pursuers followed and took the village, which that same evening was set on fire to prevent the escape or withdrawal of the inhabitants and to prevent serious plundering from occurring. We made our camp in the flat field, where there was an abundance of long reeds and grass. According to the account that the Chinese and the Formosans themselves gave us afterward, 13 of theirs remained dead and 6 were wounded, although our inhabitants had obtained no more than 9 heads, which this nation is extremely eager for. None of ours remained, and only 2 or 3 soldiers were wounded in the feet with foot traps. The next day, being the 26th of the same month, we marched again toward Saccam, passing through the aforementioned village, which was located about a quarter hour's journey from an extraordinarily large or broad but shallow river. We found everything burned, with not a single house remaining standing, and as a certain sign that the inhabitants of the aforementioned village had surprised and murdered one of our Junks [small ships] lying in the Jouckan River at night,

The aforementioned river, which at that time had become a large stretch of dry land, showed on both sides and close behind us large troops, who sought to pursue and encircle us if they could. Therefore, with a certain troop of soldiers and almost all the inhabitants, we made a proper counterattack against them. Seeing this, that we were coming at them and that they could not run as fast with their horses, they all immediately took flight without pursuing us further. And thus we came—with this outstanding victory, which was extremely highly esteemed by the surrounding villages—thank God, with a strong and healthy force, by a shorter route on the 28th of the same month again to Saccam. This having thus fortunately occurred and been accomplished, they prepared the matter through a certain Soulanger, in order to bring into our hands most of all the guilty from the aforementioned village who had been occupied with the murder of a certain sick-comforter [chaplain], as well as those who had helped carry out the enormous deed with those of Mattauw, in the most convenient manner, and thus to protect the innocent from damage.

In order to bring this about, on the 8th of January in the year 1636, we marched over Sinckan with our previous force and a good party of Sinckan inhabitants in that direction, and arrived without any resistance or opposition a little before sunset in the aforementioned village, where at first most everything had fled. However, no one who appeared was given any offense or molestation, claiming that we came in peace. 57 villages on Formosa are now satisfied with the Dutch state. The Pimabaers are a nation dwelling close by the gold mine. [We made] a cessation of weapons and [established] Pangsoia as a fortified or allied place, so that if any enemies wished to wage war in the field or appear, or in the event of the stranding or loss of any of our ships (which God forbid), they would appear with our flag among ours and thus provide all help and assistance. However, principally to make it known to them that our friends are with us, and to prevent all resulting misfortunes from occurring. This having been done, each returned with joy to his village and we departed for Fort Zeelandia. This peace alone has been binding and very strictly maintained with good contentment of each until our departure from Taijouan, which was on the 15th of November last, and has been continued. But gradually, now and then (as Your Excellency may be pleased to observe through a certain missive from Dominie Robertus Sumius addressed to Your Excellency), various other villages, some of which requested this of their own accord and some resolved to do so upon our written request, have also been brought under the common bond of peace, so that the number has increased from 22 to 57 villages, which the General Company has taken under its protection as their lords and recognized. Among these, the most notable are 15 villages located on the southern end of Formosa, whose inhabitants are called Lonckjouwers [Siraya people], who possess a good portion of the land on the east and also the west side there and wage war against a certain nation called the Pimabaers, who, according to the account of these Lonckjouwers, are also seated on the east side of the mountains a large stretch to the north of them and wage war against the inhabitants who possess the gold mine. These aforementioned Ponckjauwers are much better civilized than the inhabitants of some of the aforementioned villages. The women as well as the men all go clothed, and they are governed by a chief (whom they greatly respect) as by a sovereign prince, who enjoys his share or portion of everything that is sown or made, as well as from the hunt. And in place of tribute, he takes [a portion]. The brother of this aforementioned chief came as a hostage of ours in Taijouan to negotiate peace with us. In the meantime, there also appeared among those of Lonckjau in Taijouan the chief of Pangsoia, who also has supreme authority over some of his villages there, and is extremely great enemies with those of Fonckjauw.

These aforementioned Ponckjauwers are much better civilized than the inhabitants of some of the aforementioned villages. The women as well as the men all go clothed, and they are governed by a chief (whom they greatly respect) as by a sovereign prince, who enjoys his share or portion of everything that is sown or made, as well as from the hunt. And in place of tribute, he takes a portion. The brother of this aforementioned chief came as a hostage of ours in Taijouan to negotiate peace with us. In the meantime, there also appeared among those of Lonckjau in Taijouan the chief of Pangsoia, who also has supreme authority over some of his villages there, and is extremely great enemies with those of Fonckjauw.

text_translated_detailed: among our Dutch nation are called satins, but since the aforementioned Veelingh has already discussed this at length, we shall here speak only of the plain as well as figured, all manner of colored and black as well as white satins. The good or best black, all manner of colored as well as white plain satins are made from extraordinarily fine silk in Canton [Guangzhou] and thereabouts. The black ones weigh from 35 to 37 taels [modern equivalent: approximately 1.3-1.4 kg] according to whether they are fine or coarse in silk and are ordinarily about 30 ells [modern equivalent: approximately 18.9 meters] long. Likewise the colored as well as white ones weigh 30 to 34 taels and are long as before. These are commonly purchased here—the colored and white ones which have appeared here only sparingly thus far—at 8 to 9 reals [modern equivalent: currency unit], and the black ones according to how fine they are at 8, 9, and also well 10 reals per piece. One must not pay too much attention to the weight unless they are very fine in luster and fine in silk and well-struck in the weaving, because if the fineness or luster is lacking, the weight is then a bad sign that the silk has been damaged in the dyeing process. It is for this reason that such satins then commonly become worn in use and are inclined to tear. For some time now we have received a considerable quantity of these black satins, which, although made in Canton and previously seemed fine, have been greatly damaged in the dyeing of the silk, were loosely struck in the weaving, were over-calendered [modern equivalent: pressed with heated rollers], and moreover the greater part of the back was entirely poor and nearly unusable. Such that we were forced—as has been brought to Batavia [Jakarta]—to open these satins and the coarse-grained silk mostly entirely and to unroll them completely in order to find the good material. And the Chinese, on account of the great trouble that is attached to this, have taken an aversion to sending such defective goods here anymore, under protest that if they were to continue, we would be forced to burn everything.

To clarify in what manner and way the rich and excellent Chinese or Taiwanese trade should be preserved against certain approaching difficulties, and the Company's position and circumstances on the island of Formosa be better secured, we present this to the esteemed Governor-General Antonio van Diemen and the honored Council of India, in the most concise and brief manner possible. That the free merchants would not proceed with the principal profits or would be harmful to the Company is easy to understand, for these people, their capital being of small means, commonly seek coarse goods of great volume, for which the Company's ships to transport the same are too costly. Your Excellency's pleasant letter from Permanent Station, from which we learned with great joy that the ships Gallias and Groll with their full cargo lay ready for Japan, and moreover that the ship Wassenaer had received the cargo of Waterloose Werve and a portion of hides, such that Your Excellency was only waiting for the yacht Daman, which had not yet arrived, but on the 2nd of this month in the afternoon, near the small table of Schagen was encountered and toward evening with God's help appeared with Your Excellency in the church bay. We had hoped that the aforementioned ship Wassenaer would have been able to take much more, for which purpose the aforementioned fluyt ship Huijsduijnen with Japanese cargo, in order to proceed to the Pescadores, had been made ready and prepared. However, from Your Excellency's aforementioned letter we learned that the Council there had resolved to hold the Gallias and Groll for another 2 or 3 days and then by the arrival of the yacht Daman, to have Wassenaer in company with the aforementioned ships sail together, or if otherwise nothing appeared, to let the two ships nevertheless proceed on their journey, so it became clear to us from this that with the cargo of Daman, Wassenaer would also receive its cargo in full, which the captain of Schagen (having been consulted about this) also confirmed. text_translated_detailed: to open what has been shipped and loaded in the same. Various Officers and sailors have approached us here regarding their discharge, which we have all deferred to Your Excellency, with regard to Wassenaer & the Gallias, with the first opportunity to proceed directly to Batavia with the fatherland's return ships. Likewise the Swan, Schagen & Huijsduijnen are projected to depart for Taijouan. Your Excellency will please allow the skipper Theunis Janssen, who has requested us beforehand regarding this matter and has asked for provisions from Your Excellency as much as the service of the General Company will permit, and make him worthy of favorable treatment in his discharge. The head merchant of Sanen, who has been restored by the Esteemed Governor General and Council of India to his previous office and salary, is now being sent with Schagen in the aforementioned capacity to Your Excellency. Your Excellency will please employ and use him in the delivery and sale of goods and also in the warehouses, and likewise provide him with good instruction regarding trade matters, what fabrics, flowers, and assortments are most desired and could be drawn in the future, and likewise if anything in the fabrics recently sent is lacking in its dimensions, width and length, etc., and what should be improved there, which we have instructed the aforementioned Sanen to note down, so that upon his return here he may make a proper report to the Esteemed Mr. Johan vander Burch, and he may also be used in trade and obtain proper knowledge. Due to lack of ballast we have been forced to leave 3787 pounds [modern equivalent: approximately 1,720 kg] consisting of 791 small pieces in the fluyt ship the Swan for its return here, the more so since we are well supplied here with large quantities of Arrack, and the Company would easily receive a loss from the large shipment. Your Excellency will have the same returned here with the aforementioned fluyt ship, if it is not entered in the invoice.

Also some good fine sealing thread. And let it be remembered that in packing the cases which are sent hereward, no shoes should be packed with hats, nor should hats be packed with anything else, for the one, by reason of the moisture, and the other by reason of the grease, will damage both hat and shoes, various packages, both of cloth, perpetuanas, hats, etc. Between these, gray paper with spike and fly-smeared, is conserved for the prevention of the same, extraordinarily well, upon which Your Excellency will be pleased to provide necessities for the equipment of the naval force traveling hereward, which we request from Your Excellency to be fulfilled as diligently as possible. In particular, anchors, cables, sails, canvas, etc. Of which this past year, by reason of the spillage on the coast of China and other quarters, has been extraordinarily scarce, indeed so much so that we have not been able to make the shipment to various quarters without great concern and fear of some considerable disaster. text_translated_detailed: 3R225 Ca RCMIEP. General Antonio van Diemen, Aken, the Honorable Governor, Esteemed and Earnest Majesty, wise, foreseeing, most Generous Lord. According to the resolution in our previous letter herewith in copy dated the 5th of August last, in the ship Wasse at the Roadstead in the islands of Pehouw, on the following day with the aforementioned ship together with the Gallias and Groll set sail, and between the 27th and 28th thereof, being 22 days' journey, on account of the northerly winds and great calm before the Bank of Coetchie, God be praised, we arrived well and with pleasure we learned from the oral report of the chief merchant Larons as well as the written notes or held daily register during my absence, the Company's present constitution had no further determination in the matter of the Rouwe silk that had occurred, but the supplicant's request from the 5 imperial cities (notwithstanding that the same with many attached false and untrue statements to the detriment of the Netherlands had been delivered by the old gentleman Findad and the Imperial Council) was flatly rejected by the Council's lord Sanincked on the 3rd of April last with some reproaching reasons, the former Governor Pieter Nuijts was released from his detention, and with the first ships his departure was permitted. The Company's ships, when they desired by passing written act to the Regents of Nagasaki that no galleys should be sailing to Japan to be encountered, and to be able to depart freely, also needed no license to unload or discharge the first coming ships or ship to those of Nagasaki, but this was done by those of Firando, just as with Groll together with Wassenaer on the same day of our arrival within Firando. Here comes also by the mild gift of 200 schuyten [Dutch currency] of silver which His Imperial Majesty gave to the Dutch commissioners, which as a hood of fame rings throughout all Japan, while such a donation was never given to the Portuguese and Dutch or other foreign nations unless they were vassals.

From this you can see, related the aforementioned Regent Firando, that his Majesty cannot tolerate no violence or oppression, or rather that thus in deed according to the saying of the aforementioned Regent would have transpired, and indeed seeing the Company's constitution as it stood in better terms before, and not more their people but the Lord of Firando, to whom authority regarding this has been given by the Governor, would seek to treat us more mildly and give satisfaction, yet this matter has been communicated with some principals here, and from them it is sustained and is known to have transpired in deed. This is further confirmed by his saying, just as his Lordship also told us that his Majesty would travel upriver or go to hear the Commissioned Chinese from Siam (notwithstanding that he had previously been sent with letters of credence from his King to request from the Emperor that passage might again be granted and the junks as before be allowed to navigate there, together with further offers of friendship and alliance), had expressly forbidden and interdicted. And that for reasons his master, who had sent him, was a man whose rightful lord and king with all his family he had murdered and killed, and had unlawfully raised himself up and placed himself in the realm. On the other hand, it appeared from the particular letters to the Regents of Nagasaki that the same were written not from the king or in his name but from lesser persons, and likewise the meager and poor gift, which following this commissioned Chinese going to Siam had become accustomed and shaved some days ago, unfinished business and with his brought cargo, without being able to sell the same, except that which was necessary for sustenance and other expenses, had, departed again, being their intention at a suitable return wind to go to the Pescadores [Piscadores] or Taiwan [Tayonan] in order to undertake to sell their goods such as sapanwood, deer hides, and otherwise there, and from there to take their voyage over Quanzhou [quinam], so that thus they could still make a double journey before coming to Siam. text_translated_detailed: Copy Resolutions on the Voyage from Batavia to the Fatherland by the Esteemed Lord Governor Hansputmans and the Council of the ships Banda and New Zealand Drawn Tuesday being the 30th of December in the Year 1636 in the ship Banda lying a little north of the Long Island at anchor The Broad Council of the ships Banda, New Zealand, Zutphen, Prinswillem, and Leeuwarden, gathered and by the Esteemed Lord Putmans called upon, Gives after done reading of a certain conceived letter the same into consideration whether yet any Signs or tokens to further instruction with Goods more thorough knowledge and prevention of all abuses by attached or dismissed should be, or well that the same already conceived in that form thus over the whole Fleet divided maintained— and thereafter followed would be, A different what ration of meat and bacon above oil Vinegar and Bread one weekly moreover rice arrack and water daily over the Whole Fleet among the people should be divided. and third whether one also some under-officers assistants and Surgeons like by some the custom on the ships in the land traveling has been, also in the Cabin shall let eat or well the same on so such rations place, as the order with the ships from the Fatherland come from our Esteemed Lords and Masters 6 is also Given. — On all which points after done consideration of the Provisions over the respective fleet to the execution of the voyage — also given seriously Laid, is it for various Good insights and motives a voting Deemed good the following to wit, — Firstly the letter in that manner as the same by his — common Excellency is set thus over the Whole fleet divided And on each article after Behoove laid and observed shall be, on pain therein at Touched, who in default remains or falls The second for First over the Whole Fleet

text_translated_detailed: Piettersz Uijthoeck. Wednesday the 28th of January in the year 1637: In the ship Banda lying at anchor under Sebesse. Observed on today, yesterday, and the day before yesterday, sometimes one and sometimes two, whether English or of our ships, have been seen crosswise in the sea, and the westerly winds are still blowing so hard that the English ship London, having departed from here yesterday to make its voyage to Cape of Good Hope, has come back here to us through the storm at the anchorage, and the captain of the aforementioned ship has presented us with his boat in order to exchange some livestock such as fruit trees for refreshment for us at the coast of Sumatra, provided that the yacht Waterloose Werve also goes there to bring the livestock and otherwise back here, and if they themselves are in need of money, to advance us so much cash. So His Excellency Governor Putmans gives the council to consider seriously whether one should accept the aforementioned presentation, since there are already many sick in the two ships, and daily through the continuous rain many more are falling ill, or whether one should neglect such a thing for some considerations. Upon which, with ripe deliberation, it was unanimously agreed with His Excellency that one should let the yacht Waterloose Werve sail to the high land of Sumatra together with the English boat in order to obtain refreshment for our sick as mentioned above, to refresh them somewhat, and in the meantime wait for our ships until the 30th of this month. Zeeland gathered together, serious consideration whether, not withstanding the appointed time to wait for one another in the Table Bay (being the 25th of March), they nevertheless should not wait for the aforementioned ships until about the 14th or 15th of May coming, or as long as the council shall find good to wait here at anchor, both in order to avoid the dangers that one might encounter with our lands with such a separated fleet and costly ships, by encounter with enemies or estranged friends through separation would have to expect, as well as to prevent or correct the mutiny and difficulties that might arise much among the common people and principally on the ships coming from Suratte, or otherwise so that one might bring our Esteemed Lords and Masters speedy returns and the General Company of the heavy monthly wages of these two ships the sooner relieve, the voyage in company with the ships Banda and New Zealand (in God's name) toward the fatherland at the speediest shall begin, the more so the later one arrives at our lands the more storm and bad weather one generally has to expect there. This aforementioned proposition being considered by the council with honor and with ripe attention was found good by one Stenis with his companions and Esteemed, and was resolved that in order to avoid all dangers from enemies as otherwise as much as possible and all difficulties that might arise among the people, with the better and greater consideration to wait until the 14th or 15th of this month here at anchor for the aforementioned ships to appear, with a view to the aforementioned date, departing one however, God willing, without remarkable delay or misfortune, still in a good season of about half August in the fatherland shall be able to appear.

text_translated_detailed:
VVI5: Instruction for the Esteemed Commander Adrian Anthonis and further council members of the ships Groe, Warmont, and Huijsduijnen, according to which they shall conduct themselves upon sailing from here to Quinam [Quanzhou/Fujian] and thereafter to Batavia [Jakarta].

The Esteemed Commander and further council members are hereby made aware, according to the most recent resolution dated the 5th current, how necessary this voyage to Quinam is. The Esteemed Governors General still require prompt advice regarding Quinam's trade and the success in proceeding with the 23,580 rixdollars [modern equivalent: silver coins] of eight reals, which were recovered from the wrecked ship Grooten by his majesty's authority there, which must be obtained. Accordingly, you are all most seriously recommended to undertake your journey as soon as you have departed these waters in God's name, sailing south of the island Pekuw [uncertain: possibly Penghu/Pescadores] directly toward the coast of China, in order to pass 5 to 6 miles to the north or windward of Pedro Branca [uncertain: possibly a coastal landmark], and to bring the same into sight. From there, to take a more direct and secure course outside the islands of Machauw [Macau], Poulo Taijo [uncertain], and the like, directly toward the small islands of Tinhosa [uncertain], situated close to the great island Amoan [Amoy/Xiamen], continuing thereafter along the coast of Amoan until the same begins to stretch entirely toward the west, at which point you shall leave it and sail toward the island Campelo [uncertain], and on the south or southwest side proceed to the proper anchorage, close under the shore to drop anchor.

Should you find any Spaniards or Portuguese anchored under the aforementioned islands, you shall endeavor to bring them into your power with the least bloodshed, provided that you prevent their escape as much as possible. In the event that (their capital being of little value) his majesty of Quinam requests the restitution most urgently, such that the same might be held back to exercise trade there and to satisfy the Company's

text_translated_detailed: Mattau had placed itself under the subjection of the Dutch nation, whereupon it served them well. Then the most guilty parties were brought to us so that we might speak with them about this matter, which happened shortly thereafter, and they brought the most troublesome and culpable among them to us. After we had obtained good information about everything, indeed even their own confession from them, we held them quite firmly, with the announcement to the entire community that we had come only to punish the wicked and not the good, and consequently we would burn and raze only the houses of the evildoers. Now, if they would preserve their houses from fire, they should bring water in reserve to his side, which they accepted with gratitude by presenting the wicked and hacking their own houses to the ground, with the promise to conduct themselves henceforth as good and faithful subjects and to quit themselves thus. So that on the 9th and in the afternoon, after we had set fire to and razed several houses of these murderers, we departed again with 7 of these principal malefactors to Sinckan, where the next morning after we had arrived with the troops, these seven prisoners, as long as the Company still stood in order, in the presence of all the inhabitants, in order to set an example among these brutal heathens, we had beheaded (by three Sinckan others who were eager to do so). This having been accomplished, in the afternoon 2 or 3 of the principal instigators of the aforementioned Soelang came to negotiate peace with us. We had the points and articles upon which those of Mattau had been received in grace presented to them through Dominie Juni, so that they might lay these before their entire community, and if they approved of them, then within a few days they might appear at the Castle to make the surrender of their land and [to make their] states [known], just as those of Mattau had done.

text_translated_detailed: Noble Gentlemen, Whereas yesterday morning, as Your Excellencies will see from the enclosed copy of the letter dated the first of this month, we have continuously experienced outside of expectation such variable weather, sometimes southerly and then again northerly winds with changeable conditions, and have had burning in the Channel, so that what we had hoped and resolved—namely that the yachts Daman, Hooch Caspel, and Cleijn Bredamme would be able to depart at their appointed time for their journey to Giscadonis—could not be accomplished. This morning, when we received outside news, the wind rose in such a manner that the aforementioned yacht had no advantage to gain for its journey in that direction, as it would first have to sail northward, for which reason, having consulted with the council and found it good, we deemed it best not to keep Your Excellency waiting any longer without some news from here. Instead, we have ordered the aforementioned three yachts to proceed their journey with all possible speed directly to Batavia [modern equivalent: Jakarta]. In the meantime, we shall employ all possible means to convey the letters for the ships Peael and Bommel to Giscadonis as conveniently as possible—the sooner the better—because the tide proved so unfavorable that it was necessary to bring the yachts out of the Channel at night (with lanterns and beacons in the Channel). And since this morning we have not heard from the yacht Cleijn Bredamme, apparently driven further by the northerly wind, we have placed letters from the Honorable Joan van der Burch for the Cleijn Bredamme in the yacht Daman, hoping that the aforementioned Cleijn Bredamme will reach Your Excellency in safety. At Fort Zeelandia, the eighteenth of October 1636. Your Excellency's obedient servant, Hans Putmans.

text_translated_detailed: toward the coast to proceed without waiting for the chief merchant Johannes van der Hagen, who brought the letters on board. Consequently, Your Excellency will receive the same with the yacht Daman. Meanwhile, a sudden flying storm arose, and the aforementioned van der Hagen remained on the Daman. The lodge's boat, returning him to land, sank before the salt river, one man drowned, and the remaining men saved themselves by swimming to land. This loss of the aforementioned van der Hagen comes very badly, as otherwise we would have employed him in the trade of Quinam with the Portuguese ducats [modern equivalent: Portuguese currency], where now we must send another. The aforementioned van der Hagen was also commissioned to bring with a young man one of my lesser letters to Bommel and another from my predecessor to the Honorable Governor-General, to be brought to the rear of Caijonan, in order to advance their voyage from the Pescadores toward the coast. With this flying storm, the fluyte Warmont (which had its beams and redoubt laid in Wancan and lay under the northern reef) was also driven from its place. Item, the yacht Waterloose Werve, loaded with lime from Wancan, both were driven from their places, so that the Company would come off very badly. In case the chief officers of Warmont and the yacht Waterloose Werve allow their journey toward the coast to proceed, which we do not hope for, yet if the same should happen, they would merit being deported together, not being worthy to serve the Company, for which there are sufficient reasons, as they will not be able to bring forward a defense for not being able to sail back along the coast of China. On the instant, we are sending people to Tancoija and Tamsuij to ascertain whether they are staying there or thereabouts, and to give orders how best they shall proceed. These packets go with the under-merchant Jan Hendrixz Cracauw, over Mattauw, in order to come to Wancan, and to obtain a junk there, with which to cross over to the Pescadores, and to bring letters to both Texel and Bommel.

Heard are the captains of the yacht Daman and the junk Nangus Acqui regarding the improper stowing of the porcelain in the aforementioned Daman and aforesaid junk Mangasacq, shipped the previous year and transported from here to Siam, who have declared to us that all those same porcelains and iron pans, as otherwise here were well conditioned upon receipt, and were properly stowed in the said yacht and junk. But that on the voyage to Siam, such hard winds occurred that no sails could be carried, as when the yacht and junk were so tossed about that scarcely anyone without holding themselves well could move from one place to another. They declare the cause to be the breaking of the aforementioned goods that resulted therefrom. However, as to the fact that they would not have delivered their full number of baskets of porcelain, they attempt to prove the contrary, as Your Excellency shall be pleased to learn from the accompanying attestation (drawn up to their advantage).

text_translated_detailed: To the Honorable: Lord Governor, General, and Council of India, the Honorable, esteemed, valiant, wise, and most generous gentlemen. The foregoing is a copy of our general missive dated the 5th of October last, which Your Honored [authority] sent via the yacht Daman from Taijoan's canal, and one [copy] over the Piscadores via the ship Bommel and another of the 9th of October via the ship Texel, which we hope Your Honored [authority] will have received well before the receipt of this, and the 5 ships and yachts with their loaded goods will have arrived safely. That in the coming [time] we would gladly like to learn [about], the fluyt Warmont, which on the 8th [of this month], lay at anchor under two anchors beneath the northern reef, was driven away in the flying storm that came, from the moment the anchor cable of its duty broke, and the daily anchor dragged after it and did not want to hold. Thus it came to rest below Tancoija, remaining then in fear, because it was provided with no more than 2 anchors. The officers might easily have let it proceed along the coast, and thus would have deprived us of the 40 beams and part of the lime that were in it, and would have driven the Company to such damage. Whereby we here could have sent a fluyt's ship's cargo for the Fatherland's return at less cost and would have remained here. Regarding this, Your Honored [authority] wrote that then [the officers] should be deported on account of pay and quality, since the aforementioned officers assured us that Your Honored [authority] could not show sufficient reasons why they could not have stopped it again. Thus the aforementioned officers would have made themselves worthy of such punishment. But since the contrary was done and the proper means were taken at hand, whereby also on the 12th of October [they] came up and entered into the canal, namely the land of Tancoija, where anchor ground is, where it with a northerly storm made an upper wall

I cannot refrain from adding here a remarkable account of this people: how easily and with what little difficulty these natives could be governed, how willingly they leave their disputes and quarrels to be decided by our appointed commissioners, how willing and ready they show themselves to be in wanting to help us against our enemies. How properly they allow themselves to be instructed in the Christian faith by Dominie Junio, those who have already had a foretaste of the said faith, and how readily even those who are still strange to this faith present themselves. When the aforementioned Junio asks them whether they are also well disposed to reject their idolatry in order to serve the one true God, all this is remarkable, and would not be accepted by many discerning minds, unless they were first informed of their natural disposition, without which no one with good judgment could speak of it. In order then to govern this nation well, Dominie Junio has until now attended to the political matters satisfactorily, but continues to persist in wanting to be relieved of them as soon as possible. And although we, according to Your Excellency's serious recommendation, would gladly see him relieved of them, various persons could be employed for this purpose

text_translated_detailed: Most Esteemed, Mighty, Generous, Wise, Provident, Discreet Lord General, the enclosed is a copy of my most recent particular letter dated the 8th of October last, sent from Wanckan from the Pescadores by the ship Texel, which I hope will have reached Your Excellency before the receipt of this, and the 5 ships and yachts will have arrived safely at the coast, which we shall be pleased to learn in due time. Since then we have with great longing looked out every day for the 2 Chinese junks from Jochoo and Jockruij, which according to long-standing rumor were said to be loaded very expensively with about 500 to 600 piculs of raw Chinese silk, various silk pieces and other goods. Upon the 10th of this month, God be praised, beyond our expectation, so soon the ships Galleasse, Schagen, and Huijsduijnen arrived in Japan here at the northern reef with a cargo of 1,039,888 guilders, 6 shillings, 11 pence, consisting of 360 taels of shuttle money, 300 bales of white stamped rice, 725 piculs of sungij planks and 2,625 [uncertain: unit of measurement] of buffaloes, from which I have taken out and credited to the general comptoir, and have left for Batavia therein 12,525 catties of plate copper, together with 42,692 catties of staff iron. Thereupon from the writing of the Esteemed President Couckebacke we learned the desired state for the Company there, namely how the petitioners of the 5 emperor's cities in their request, to the detriment of the Company, had been flatly rejected, that the Company's ships were permitted to depart as they desired, provided that passing acts [of safe conduct] showed no Portuguese galleons between Macao and Japan to be encountered, to avoid damage, that by means of his long imprisonment he was released, how we no longer had to address ourselves to the regents of Nangaracquij in unloading the ships, but to those of Firando, how we had obtained an honorable title in that we had received an audience with his Emperor's Majesty,

text_translated_detailed: According to the opinion of Captain Hambuan, it would be of too great consideration to undertake any evil attempt to obstruct the Chinese trade, as it would be resigned to such a small matter. I humbly request that Your Excellency be pleased to take into closer consideration the lightening of pepper from the departing junk bound for China, and to set apart what has passed as a sign of what fruits it can bear, so that if Your Excellency finds the neglect to be most advisable, yet without being pleased to give contrary orders in the ship's instructions to the captains of the ships, so that all misfortunes and causes of irritation that might befall the rich Chinese trade would be removed and the trade might be conserved for the Company. We wish therefore to trust that my advice will be received by Your Excellency as fatherly and as paternal as I, according to my judgment, find it to belong to the service of the general Company from the heart. With this, Your Excellency's most earnest, stalwart, generous, and most discreet manner of foresight, may God pray that Your Excellency be conserved in His well-beloved and long-lasting health and that Your Excellency be granted a fortunate, prosperous, and desired governance. In Fort Zeelandia [Anping, Taiwan], on the 14th of November 1636. Your Excellency's dutiful servant was signed Johan van der Burgh.

To the Honored, Esteemed, Stalwart, General, and Wise Counselors of Foresight, Most Generous Gentlemen:

The foregoing is a copy of our latest [letter] to Your Excellency sent with the Bredamme and the fluyt Warmont yesterday evening, at which time I promised the Lord Governor Putmans that this morning I would allow the fluyt Schagen (to which three hundred canassos [uncertain: possibly a unit of measurement or commodity] of sugar, its water, and some victuals were still lacking) to follow, with which we were occupied that night and this morning in order to arrange the said effect. These then are the reasons why I have had this latest general missive written by two hands, so that in case the Schagen should arrive before the Bredamme and Warmont, since our latest [letter] was sent with the 5 yachts and ships on the 8th and 14th of October last, Your Excellency would not lack advice from us. Accordingly, the same is amplified with these few rules, as Your Excellency must expect further writing with the ship the Galliasse, which shall follow as soon as it is able. And so that Your Excellency might have knowledge of what has been shipped in the Bredamme and Warmont, in case this fluyt ship Schagen should arrive alongside the aforementioned 2 ships, enclosed herein is the copy of the invoice and bills of lading of the ships Bredamme and Warmont loaded with the following, namely: 22,123 catties [modern equivalent: approximately 1,327 kg] of white raw Chinese silk; 76,076 pieces of various porcelain; 1,601,650 catties of white sugar; 55,970 catties of brown sugar; 4,740 planquins [uncertain: possibly a type of fabric or commodity]; 1,783 taels [modern equivalent: approximately 67 kg] of black gold; 12,000 pieces of musk with one [uncertain: unclear measurement]; 35 pieces of Bengali slaves; 3 basins. Our latest [letter] to Your Excellency was sent with the fluyts the Swan, Schagen, and Huisduinen, dated the 15th of August last, which I hope will have arrived there with pleasure before the receipt of this, and Your Excellency will have received the same, wherein I advised Your Excellency of the events of our voyage and as specified hereafter, how on the 29th of July, at the latitude of 22 degrees and 22 minutes, around 4 o'clock in the afternoon between Macao and Lamoa, we had seen 4 ships which lay with their sails set aside and waiting for us, and we thought they were our ships. text_translated_detailed: Copy 3 July. Since the Commander through the skippers of the 75-day register kept by the Commander Jan van der Burgh, Councillor of the Indies, during the voyage that with the Ship Bredamme [normalized version: Bredamme], on 3 July in the year 1636, in company with the fluyt [expanded: light sailing vessel] the Swaen [normalized version: the Swan], and the yacht Hoogcaspel departed from the roadstead of Batavia [normalized version: Jakarta], in order to advance the journey to Tayouan [normalized version: Taiwan], in the morning around nine o'clock we sailed from the roadstead of Batavia with the land wind, set our course north by east, in order to run by the east of the islands of Ontough Java [normalized version: Ongkong/Onrust], and as soon as we had passed the unrest, we formed a Council of War from the chief officers of the aforementioned ships, where all matters that might occur would be handled, and we found it good to establish an equal order, that is one portion of rice for each man per day, item two days per week, meat and bacon to be given, namely ¾ pound of meat for each man and half a pound of bacon as before, for each man per week, likewise ½ mug of oil and an equal half mug of vinegar for each man per week we shall give, in order that our provided provisions may stretch as needed. And in order to conserve our water we shall also give a ration of one flask of water to each man per day. However, as soon as we became aware of them, they were held back by the wind, from which it became quite clear that they were not free-sailing vessels. We attempted to sail them with greater effort using sail-handling and other means, and we identified them around four hours after midday as four Portuguese merchant vessels, which were making their voyage from Malacca to Macao. Three of them had by evening drifted so far to leeward that it was impossible for us to reach any of them, so we continued to pursue two of them. text_translated_detailed: We were sailing past the island Amain. In the afternoon we had a latitude of 15 degrees and 50 minutes. In the evening we found ourselves alongside the island Tindosa, about five miles away. Here there is high land to the northwest on the aforementioned island Amau, and to the east of the high land you have low land again, and it appears as if they were all islands, but they are connected to one another, as we sailed past them. On the same day, in the morning the wind was from the southwest with stiff breeze, and fair weather. We saw, a few hours after sunrise, a sail behind us to the southwest of us that was running before the wind with our course. We found it good to wait for it, and to that end we took in all our sails and bound them with bands to the rigging. Thus, with the proper signal to the fluyt and the yacht Hoostasper, it was also ordered that if it were a foreign sail, we would not be seen by them until we were sufficiently close, and if their course changed, we would have to consider whether it might well be an unfree vessel [a pirate or enemy ship], which we would pursue and see what the time would bring about. Thus, waiting for it until the glass [watch period] passed, which through the spyglass, below from our ship, we could see to be a Portuguese ship, which showed itself very high with two masts and two topsails. It also shortly thereafter tacked to the wind in order to get away from us. text_translated_detailed: Concerning our ships, or whether they might be free-sailing vessels, leaving behind the flag staff on the Company's behalf, the prince's flag waving, to warn the fluyt, the sloop, and the yacht Hooch Caspel, according to his letter, and since the aforementioned sails had drawn very close to the northern sun, because all of them were trying to escape the wind, and only Bredamme sailed better than the fluyt and the yacht, and also the foreign vessels sailed with the wind, so we were able to pursue them for so long that we could recognize what free-sailing vessels they might be. We understood that friends did not need to flee from us. Meanwhile, with the skipper Minne Willemisz and our communication, we applied all possible diligence in the matter of setting sails, and everything that a diligent skipper and careful seaman could have contributed, for the reason that we approached the aforementioned vessels three hours before sunset so closely that we could see their large broad sails and double bonnets, and also sharp pennants, which would well have been recognizable as great Portuguese ships, which we presumed were coming from Malacca and heading toward Quanzhou or Macau for their voyage. One of the same sails was very confused, wanting then to run before us and then again to the wind, whereby we came even closer to them. The other three scattered so far to leeward that in the night, although there was clear moonlight, it would grow dark for us, and consequently we could see less in order to be able to sail after them. From a missive dated from the standing [position] in Wanckan from the upper merchant of The Hague, it is understood how certain captains of the Chinese in Vovorolang had appeared on the 29th of August in Wanckan, relating how 180 to 190 Vovorolese had betaken themselves to the Chalk Island in flight in order, when opportunity arose, to attempt something on the wooden fort Wambas there or indeed to set it on fire. Likewise, how since our made insinuation dated the 14th of February last past, the Chinese in place of being harsh now have many of their people treated well. This village Vovorolang would consist of 344 houses and about 1000 able-bodied men, with 400 of them under a certain Captain Sterk to make it so that when opportunity arose they could separate themselves from the others and come to dwell in Wanckan under our protection. The said Captain or captain having placed beforehand a letter at his house so that whenever something was attempted on this village by our Nation, it might remain spared. Of all this, time provides the 14th of the same, not without having passed favorable wind with reasonable weather. text_translated_detailed: Anthony van Diemen from the date of the 12th of November, ambassador and further attached papers. 459. Excellency, Earnest, Manly, wise, Generous Lord. To the Honorable Lord Governor General, My Lord, Your Excellency's very pleasant letter of the 30th of May 1636 reached us with the arrival of the Honorable President Nicolaes Couckebacker under the island Champelo on the 25th of June, following thereafter (with the ships Grol, Huijsduijnen, and Daman), and from it we understood with great pleasure that we had been provided with proper copies of instructions for the procurement or recovery of the 23,580 reals of eight and reichsdaalers [modern equivalent: silver coins] from the wrecked ship Grootenbrouck by the Honorable Governor Putmans, and it grieves us greatly that our commission in this matter has not been able to accomplish more. It is thus that we, following our instructions and insofar as knowledge from the Almighty has been granted to us, have neglected no diligence in this matter, but have worked everything to the best of our ability, which Your Excellency shall clearly see from the following. Our arrival, together with the Honorable Major Ariaen Anthoonisen, was on the 6th of March in the year 1636 in the Baxe Thoron, and after we had learned of the death of the old king and the resumption of possession by the young King, in the trading place Praijphoo, which had occurred a few days before, as can be verified in our most recent letter sent on the 29th of March in the year 1636, we appeared again on board, and after an examination of the situation there had been made, the aforementioned Honorable Major convened the Council and proposed that, since we had received permission from the nearest Councilor of the King, we might freely land our merchandise (if we had any), for which suitable places had been assigned to us, or whether, following this, although it was contrary to our instructions and hastily done, it should not have been done, considering that the monsoon was mostly past, such costly ships as the Groll and Warmondt on that same day, being the 13th of March, should set sail for Batavia—

text_translated_detailed: Before the King having come, and proper Reverence having been done, he had us sit down after old custom, as when we presented to his Majesty with proper Respect in short the tenor of Your Excellency's missive, likewise if there was anything displeasing therein, that we might be pleased to open that matter, considering that our commander with his ships under the island Champelo remained waiting for our reciprocal [dealings], who was expressly sent to settle all disputes in the best manner with his Majesty under proper conditions so that we might continue to frequent the trade in his land, and the same remain unmolested from threatening evils, by whatever means this could be secured, we did not doubt that his Majesty could have understood thoroughly from Your Excellency's missive. The King answered that he could understand the content of Your Excellency's letter very well, consequently he deemed it unnecessary to repeat the same again, it would also be reasonable and just that Your Excellency recover the called-in 23,580 reales together with the goods and further small items that were demanded, yet since he had never seen anything of it, much less enjoyed it, and everything had passed into his possession, and he had brought the kingdom under his rule with weapons, he could therefore not understand any restitution, yet if Your Excellency wished to wage war in his land, he could not prevent it, for he lacked neither cannons nor power to resist. Without touching the threat of Tonquin in the least, but let the same pass unnoticed, if Your Excellency would also be pleased to let commerce in his land continue, it stood in both Your Excellency's good pleasure. Item they declared so if Your Excellency would be pleased to let the trade in Senua continue to proceed, that the same could first be pursued by no one other than us, but regarding the restoration of the 23,580 reales of eight [reales], he could not understand it, and would also not be spoken to about it anymore.

Missive from the King's Majesty of Quinam to the Dutch King. Since the 19th. I have read in the old records and found that the righteous Kings have their kingdoms to govern with light, and that they keep the entire world or all nations far and near as their friends and allies. My honored father and ancestor was a truly mighty Lord and King, maintaining peace and correspondence with the Netherlanders, not knowing that there were any evil subjects of His Excellency or of the land. However, as Annembij was a great officer, he sought to pursue his particular profit. Thus, with the sending of the Netherlanders, the deceased King and my aforementioned honored father was able to skillfully close his eyes, so that he neither saw nor had the slightest knowledge of it. However, I have caused the aforementioned Annembij to be punished for his evil deeds with death and had him cut into small pieces, as an example to many. Now it is that afterward from the Dutch King a certain envoy has been committed to me, dealing with the differences that occurred before, and bringing with him a gift to me, consisting of twenty pieces of silver, two pieces of cloth, forty rolls of damask, ten red gielams [uncertain: type of fabric], two robes, and two Corgie gouseratsche [uncertain: type of clothing], for which I thank you, Esteemed Lord. text_translated_detailed: 481. Enclosed herewith are copies of my previous letters dated the 13th of November last, and further the accompanying papers. Missive from the Majesty of the King of Quinam to the Dutch King. Almighty Lord. I have read in the old authors and found that righteous kings have their kingdoms to govern with light, and that they hold all the world or all nations far and near as their friends and allies. My honored father and ancestor was a righteous and mighty King and Lord, maintaining peace and correspondence with the Netherlanders, not knowing that there were any wicked subjects of his Excellency or of the land's lord. But Annembij, being a great officer, sought to pursue his particular profit. Thus, with the sending of the Netherlanders, the deceased King and my mentioned honored father was very skillfully made to close his eyes, so that he saw nothing in the selling, or at the very least had any knowledge of it. But I have punished the aforementioned Annembij for his wicked deeds with death, and had him cut into small pieces as an example to many. Now it is that afterwards a certain envoy from the Dutch King has been sent to me, committed to the same, dealing with differences that have occurred before these matters, and bringing me a gift consisting of fifty pieces, standing in twenty pieces of silver, two pieces of cloth, forty rolls of damask, ten red gielams, two coats, contrary and two Corgie Guoseratsche cloth. For this I am grateful to your Excellency. I beseech that the King of Holland, with his great magnanimity and divine heart, show favor to my father and to me, so that the previous differences and disputes need not be remembered anymore, but rather to the contrary, with my principles of governance, the friendship and correspondence may be renewed in his Majesty.

text_translated_detailed: of Missive from the Majesty of the King of Quinam to the Dutch King. Almighty Lord. I have read in the old authors and found that righteous kings have their kingdoms to govern with light, and that they hold all the world or all nations far and near as their friends and allies. My honored father and ancestor was a righteous and mighty Lord and King, maintaining peace and correspondence with the Netherlanders, not knowing that there were any wicked subjects of his Excellency or of the land's lord. But Annembij, being a great officer, sought to pursue his particular profit. Thus, with the sending of the Netherlanders, the deceased King and my mentioned honored father was very skillfully made to close his eyes, so that he saw nothing, or at the very least had any knowledge of it. But I have punished the aforementioned Annembij for his wicked deeds with death, and had him cut into small pieces as an example to many. Now it is that afterwards a certain envoy from the Dutch King has been sent to me, committed to the same, dealing with differences that have occurred before these matters, and bringing me a gift consisting of twenty pieces of silver, two pieces of cloth, forty rolls of damask, ten red gielams, two coats, and two Corgie Guoseratsche cloth. For this I am grateful to your Excellency. I beseech that the King of Holland show his great magnanimity and divine heart toward my father and me, so that the previous differences and disputes need not be remembered anymore, but rather to the contrary, with my principles of governance, the friendship and correspondence may be renewed in his Majesty. Furthermore, I make another request to your Excellency, that it may please you to allow all young men who frequent my land, both coming and going, and the subjects of your Excellency to conduct their trade unharmed and unmolested. If then such is understood and followed by your Excellency, the friendship shall certainly continue unbroken between Holland and Guinam forever.

text_translated_detailed: I have observed in the old authorities that truth far exceeds lies. All the lands and peoples who previously were under the obedience of my honored father now belong entirely to me, and whoever comes to my gate is received in a friendly manner. However, among my subjects I had a wicked and cunning scoundrel named Annembij, who knew how to blind my father and completely obscure the matter of the Netherlands. Thus it happened that my father passed away. Being informed of the wickedness of Annembij, I had him put to death. The Netherlanders from Taijuhan have come and have declared to me much good regarding your person and state in Taijuhan, and your Excellency has presented me with a gift, consisting of half a piece of red cloth, ten rolls of damask, Moleuw, half a Co gielam [uncertain: specific textile measure], half a Corge [uncertain: specific textile measure], and half a Corgie guserats cloth. I am heartily grateful to your Excellency for this and request that your Excellency be pleased to recommend me to the King of Holland, so that we may continue together in an unbreakable friendship and alliance. If your Excellency is so inclined, Quinam and Holland shall always remain as one body. Furthermore, I send you five Quinamse armosines, one Cattij Calamback [uncertain: specific textile measure], and two elephant tusks. Received per one wanckan Adij. P.M. [post meridiem] May 1st, Year 1636. In Batavia.

On the first of June last, departing from the roadstead before Batavia according to Your Excellency's order, we passed on the 5th of that month at the Strait of Salaambang, arriving on the 10th of that month in the morning according to the arranged plan. Since the fluyt ship Huijsduijnnen [Huijsduijnnen] was in poor condition and needed to be better ballasted, we anchored under Poulo Lauro [Pulo Lauro], and from there we continued our voyage in the afternoon. On the 24th of that same month, under the Island of Chiampello [Chiampello], having previously, about 8 miles south of the River of Phaijphoo [Phaijphoo], ordered the yacht Daman to sail at night before that river, in order to fetch from there Your Excellency's instructions and further papers, to the Chief Merchant Abraham Suijcker [Abraham Suijcker] with the boat through one of the under-merchants who had previously been in Phaijphoo, and to give notice of our company's arrival, with orders to the aforementioned Suijcker to proceed with all haste under Chiampello on board, which happened that same day in the evening. text_translated_detailed: During the time of the presence of the head merchant Paron, this occurred, but in response such matters were received, and similar things were not new, nor could they, and shall not make the Portuguese more odious, nor the Company more advanced, for His Majesty has sufficiently knowledge of all their deeds and dealings through their own writings and renegade priests, and following that, such persecution of the followers of the priests and Christians throughout the entire Kingdom of Japan in order to root them out once and for all was put into effect, just as daily experience teaches us. Among other things, in April last past, a sharp investigation was conducted within the city of Edo [Tokyo] among the lepers, blind and crippled people, and eighty-three Christians, both men and women, persons, children old and young, who were all enclosed together within a palisade made expressly outside the city, and strictly guarded from without until they had all perished from hunger. Likewise, with the departure of the four galleons from Nagasaki [Nagasacqe] to Macao, two hundred eighty-seven persons were sent, both men, women, and children, not only of Portuguese descent but also those who had been held by the Portuguese for several years and subsequently had been married to Japanese [Tappanders], and had five, six, or more children, where they were forced to abandon the same and their husbands. Also among the same Japanese, because they had taken half-caste children as their own and had done the same, they were sent along. For Captain Moor (who until the departure of the galleons was, along with others, furnished in the new building, is now in the city to excuse the great guard, a smaller dwelling well palisaded and provided with a guardhouse is being prepared). What goods this year have been brought to the market with the four galleons, Your Excellencies shall be pleased to take note from the attached Memorandum presented to us by the Regent Phesodo [uncertain: possibly a Japanese official's name].

In the evening, late around 9 o'clock, we learned that his Excellency had returned. We went immediately to his lodging, but could not come to speak with him, he excused himself greatly before us, saying that he had been very tired, and that he would have us summoned tomorrow. We were welcome, etc.

On the 20th of the same month we went to the house of the Lord of Firando, where we appeared before his Excellency for the first time. He said he was glad about our arrival. He would immediately write a letter to the Councillor Tackmond and let his Highness know of our arrival. He further asked how we had tarried so long, what rarities we had brought for his Majesty, whether Captain Couckebacker had also departed. To which we answered that the inclination to come up earlier had been good, but since it had pleased his Excellency to allow it, we would freely and at our leisure first dispatch all the ships, and then come up to pay our respects, which is what happened. We left him with the understanding that when at the time as we appeared here last year, it would have been timely enough, which now has happened 8 days earlier. Regarding the rarities for his Majesty, his Excellency would have the Councillor Hannicked present to his Majesty the release of Pieter Nuyts. The Governors of Nagasaki had taken offense at the Hollanders, and the commissioned [representatives] were sent to the aforementioned Governors in order to learn of their discontent. Complaints of the aforementioned Governor to the commissioned [representatives]. Sustained and declared March, Year 1636. Immediately send the memorandum. Item: The Captain had departed, as we had informed his Excellency from Miako. Finally we came to the matter concerning the release and situation of the Lord Nuyts, which showed us disconsolate and poorly satisfied that there had still come no end to it. We recommended and asked his Excellency most humbly that his matter might be concluded on this journey. His Excellency was pleased to point out means and ways, and we would not fail to pursue everything that lay within reason and would not be neglected by us. It had lasted so long and we had been fed so long with promises that bore no fruit that we had come to the end of counsel and belief to place our hope. His Excellency gave us great comfort, saying it grieves me that it cannot be otherwise. Yet take good courage. The Councillor Sanickod has taken the matter upon himself to serve his Majesty. Do not doubt that on this journey you will, like his release, obtain [it]. text_translated_detailed: 1636: In Edo, on the 2nd of May, the 4th of April was given, we should prepare ourselves for that time. Following this, the Lord of Firando spoke: these people are very eager to know what prospect there is regarding the matter of raw silk, whether they will be able to avoid this burden, or whether the people of the request, who are soliciting for it, have to expect or wait for it. It would be desirable that His Majesty knew the ground and substance of the pancado of the silk completely. It would soon be remedied, for His Majesty's profit, honor, nor service is furthered thereby, much less the common good. All the foreigners sitting under the pancado will bring no silk to Japan, for the people who make such voyages do not intend to do so in order to lose, which remains with the Portuguese and Chinese, however little the price is, which is brought by them to the market. On the contrary, if they were relieved of the burden of the pancado, they would import silk in greater abundance, which now does not happen. The Dutch, likewise bringing no silk, and the Japanese or domestic silk not being sufficient, and will it not then fall heavily upon the people, when they must pay as much for one robe as they do now for several? etc. The Governor's Highnesses answered: it is true, all of that is not known to His Majesty. In case the Councillors generally resolved to make His Majesty aware of the same, and to examine this matter near Nantgan, it would undoubtedly not remain thus long, for His Majesty is so liberal, honor-loving, and unspeakably wealthy, that he would in no way desire his subjects to suffer anything improper from the foreigners. Until now we have also not been able to understand or resolve to allow the request regarding the pancado

text_translated_detailed: so far in the hatred of the community, and that principally in the disgrace of Your Excellency, that we do not know what we shall undertake and begin to defend our innocent cause. This harmful burden is surely not to the service of His Majesty, nor to the benefit of the common good. What then may be the cause that this happens, and if it was unknown to Your Excellency, we wish to relate under reverence how it has gone with us in former times until these three most recent years, when the Dutch were able to give their silk, for as much as Your Excellency could bargain for, and to those who wished it. In that time the high authorities were able to be content. To which as answer we asked: no, it is unnecessary that the selling of your silk neither serves nor benefits the common good. I can well understand that, but since it is a matter entrusted by His Majesty, which order from His Majesty once given is not so lightly changed and can be, you must have patience in this and await the time, from which changes are born. Furthermore, His Excellency asked whether we Christians were, and what the difference was between our religion and Portuguese teaching and ours. We answered: Yes, that we were also Christians, and the difference between Portuguese teaching and ours was such and so profound that the same could not be explained so quickly. However, one matter Your Excellency would be pleased to consider: how great the difference must be, namely when the Spanish and Portuguese in former times had taken from us any castle, city, or territory, they forced the people to accept their teaching, and those who could not understand it, they killed in a very shameful manner in many ways. His Excellency asked: do they not do that now also? We answered: they would gladly, but cannot, for in place of that they used to damage and take from us very harmfully, fortune has turned so much in our favor that we have not only retaken our lost lands and cities, but take still yearly from their lands and splendid cities and castles. He asked: how long has the war with them lasted? Answer: over 10 years. He asked: why do the English not come to Japan at present? Answer: because in Japan, since they do not have the Chinese trade, there is no profit for them to gain. He asked: why do you rob together with the English now on the sea? Answer: that we never robbed, nor were we any robbers, but that we sought to do damage to our enemies, both on the sea and on land. And in case such speech of the Dutch went forth, that was spread by our enemies—damage and harm (we said) we must and shall do to our enemy, whereby we are praised by all the great potentates of the world, that possessing so small a land we have been so courageous as to save ourselves from the deceitful papal Spanish nets. His Excellency's speech from the 11th to the 12th Japanese month is an investigation and description concerning the 66 lands in Japan, which investigation, which was strict, in the province Ōsaka

text_translated_detailed: 127: in number, which Your Excellencies would be pleased to review alongside this document. The reasons why we have become enemies with the Spanish and Portuguese, we shall explain to Your Excellencies briefly. The King of Spain and Portugal sent his ambassadors into our land with this proposal: "You Hollanders are my neighbor; I have resolved to present to you my friendship and request that we may henceforth live together as good and faithful friends." This presentation we accepted and held as sincere and genuine, and we found that under this cloak of friendship, more and more a great number of priests from their side came over into our land. And they established their churches everywhere and in all cities, and sought through their faith, which they spread at that time, to incorporate our land with subtle cunning. When we learned of this, it resolved us to banish all the priests and their followers from our land and to forbid their faith. Since that time, we have been and remain in enmity with Spain and Portugal, and we have waged war against one another now for over 70 years, both at sea and on land, sparing no places. And as we understand, it has been reported to Your Excellencies, to our sorrow, that we are robbers and that we take our enemies solely to rob them. We also hear that Your Excellencies understand that we rob the Chinese on the sea and are in fact nothing other than robbers. We say this is untrue. In former times we were inclined to be able to trade in the land of China, and to this end, and to request this, we sent our commissioned ambassadors into China, through whom we were answered that foreign ships and people we do not allow in our land. However, if you wish to come with your ships to the island of Rougaen [Formosa], there we will trade with you and show you satisfaction. On this promise, His Excellency found it good to set down the aforementioned document, although the Chief Merchant Caron wished to bring something against it. Thus it was established and delivered in April of the year 1636 in Tedo [Edo], and a contract was closed. We sent a good number of ships and a rich capital to the aforementioned Pehou [Penghu], but we found that they dealt with us in all things very cunningly and deceived us with all manner of lies. Indeed, instead of granting us trade, they finally took our ships, money, and people, whom they very shamefully burned and murdered. Since that time, we have, in revenge and vengeance, taken some of theirs, whatever we could seize from them. Regarding this, those of China sent their ambassadors back to us in Sacatra [Surat] with this address: "The island Pehou lies under the jurisdiction of China and consequently we may not tolerate foreigners there. But if you wish to settle on the island Formosa in the harbor of Taijouan, then we will bring you the fullness of merchant goods according to your wishes." This contract, newly closed from both sides, has kept our trade with those of China established until now. Far from us and from what we are, we take or injure no one other than our open enemies. 37th month, 7th day. To the governing lords. From François Caron. Foreword or justification of ours.

text_translated_detailed: The giving of thanks to his Regent, and his response. On the 2nd of May we went to the house of his Excellency, in order to thank his Lordship for the good news from yesterday, which having been done, his Excellency related, among other reasons, the state and situation of Mr. Nuits' release, how the Counselor Samikede had taken the matter upon himself to serve his Majesty, but that God once again prevented such, whereupon we answered, so we see and perceive well enough that this man will not easily be released, which is indeed a sorrowful matter. His Excellency said no, you must not throw it so far, it will nevertheless come soon enough, but you need not wait for that reason, but as soon as you shall have obtained an audience, then hasten yourself quickly from here, for there have already been too many days in which such matters of governance have been handled, much less will anything else be handled or attended to from now on, except the preparation of his Majesty's departure. I was made aware that the Lord of Firando [Hirado] was ordered to appear in the collegiate gathering, in order to make a comparison and declaration of the situation, the declaration of the Dutch to make, but the gathering was never held due to many occupations, nor shall it be held for a long time, his Majesty will, according to all appearances, on the 13th of this fourth month, being the 11th of May, depart from here, and on the same day return, having returned, there will be 1 or 2 months, but so much with feasts, games, comedies, churches, and divine services, guests and various rejoicings to be done, that from any of the foreign lands, the Dutch being able to the land of Japan as the Portuguese do with fabrics adorned their way from Macao well nor entirely cut off. His Majesty in the evening would send the Interpreter to learn what answer had come from there, of which I here set down the extract. Your Excellency's recommendation regarding the Dutch license, I have well understood; there is so much to do that such small trifling matters cannot well find a place. After that I shall present it to His Imperial Majesty tomorrow. On the 11th, the Lord of Firando [Hirado] sent us a messenger and had him inform us of the license to depart, and that we should send the Interpreter from the Castle early tomorrow morning to receive the ordinary gift from His Majesty given to the Dutch, and to hear the given word regarding the license, that the Dutch shall depart again. On the 12th, early in the morning, the Interpreter went to the Castle, where he was informed by Councillor Tackionde that His Majesty had yesterday granted the Dutch license to depart again. He also gave him a written document to receive in the storehouse of the Commander thereof twenty silk robes, which all happened accordingly. After the Interpreter had returned, we went to thank the Lord of Firando for the gift accepted by all the Councillors. Arrival of the commissioned one in Firando, May, Year 1636: We went to Tedo to his house, where he wished us good fortune over this favorable circumstance and recommended us to depart at the earliest opportunity and not to wait anywhere else. On that date we requested permission from the Regents to dispatch our commissioner, to which we received the answer that their letters and the nobleman whom they would send with him were not yet ready, therefore we had to wait from day to day and from morning to morning. On the 11th the interpreter was to go again to the Regents to request that the commissioned Hollander might depart speedily. We regret that the expression of thanks for this great favor proceeded so slowly. As for the answer, they still had to consult with one another, to write and arrange matters, and as soon as these were ready they would let us know. In our letters to the Lord of Firando, we recommended to His Excellency that, as it seemed fitting to His Honor, it would be advisable that some gifts be given to His Majesty's messenger or to the Councillors as a sign of gratitude. We suggested that His Excellency in such circumstances would be pleased to act in such a manner as he would find best to satisfy the Japanese high authorities and to honor the Dutch. The reasons why no gifts were sent with the Hollander were these: First, that there were no goods presently in the warehouse suitable for gifts, but all had been sold, and we did not know to whom, how much, and what had been given away. Therefore we had no commission to buy any in Macao, and principally also we did not know whether gifts should be given or whether His Excellency would have the matter entirely set aside. We therefore requested that His Excellency would be pleased to provide or have procured such goods in Edo as he would find necessary. text_translated_detailed: We shall refute such matters, so it appears that our reasoning has gained no credence with Your Excellency, which grieves us. After this, if it pleases Your Excellencies to hear us once more, we declare what the matter is: we are people who possess our own land under good governance and laws, conducting our trade throughout the entire world, indeed as far as Japan, and we harm no one except our enemy the King of Spain, whom we fight most vigorously and from whom we take lands, goods, and people annually. The Regent spoke: "How is it that you nevertheless take from the Chinese, and complaints come to our ears daily?" We answered: "It is not so, but rather that we have sought to serve China with all possible means and to help them, just as this has indeed happened many times, in that we have used our ships and all war materials for their service and against the inland pirates, and we still steadily wish to find a remedy to turn their goodwill toward us." Thereupon the Regents or Governors declared that they expected nothing from their Excellencies but from those of Firando [Hirado] regarding the Company's trade negotiations. July, Year 1636. In Firando, we would obtain as many goods as our capital can reach, and since we are theirs, we would wish to cause them no offense or displeasure. The reason being that we sought the trade (after we had sought it with many different methods and friendliness, as well as services to the land for a long time and found we could not obtain it, but were most shamefully deceived) also through war, but not through robbery. For if we gave those of China the slightest occasion for displeasure and took but a single vessel of theirs, our trade would immediately be closed, whereby we would then sit with such great capital and ships without being able to accomplish anything with them.

We went to the house of the President of that place, where we were also treated in a friendly manner and delivered our gift. His Excellency also recommended to us to be well on our guard and to give each person as little reason for complaint as was possible, for, said he, you have many enemies. Having received our leave, we went to inspect the lodge or prison of the Portuguese, which is a work that in the bay of Nagasaki on the south side has been raised from the water of stone and earth, long about a stadium or 600 feet, and 240 feet wide. Their dwelling upon arrival is round about with a closely woven fence, wherein stand two rows of houses and a street in the middle, having a bridge to go from the land onto this island, and a water gate through which the Portuguese shall pass twice in a voyage, namely once when they go from their galleons and once when they board ship again, without being permitted to set their foot further outside.
