Yesterday we rode until two o'clock in the evening to Ockabee, thirteen miles. The last quarter [of the day] on the 31st, Monday morning, the wind was from the east, the weather clear. We rode along the other side, passed through a large mountain range and through a great drainage area, and [passed] the city of Suxinga where a large castle lies. We lodged in Eesux, then rode along the South Sea and the hot strand of the corner mountain range, all of which led us to the city of Cambaex, having ridden ten miles.

In the name of the Lord, 1636: on the land route to Gedou in Japan, the first of January 1636, Tuesday morning, the wind was clear, the weather fair. We passed three swift-running rivers with a bridge approximately a musket shot from the South Sea. We lodged in Jsolbaxe, rode through three or four rivers, and arrived in the evening in the city of Mjssima at the imperial mountain range of Falconry, having ridden nine miles.

The 2nd, Wednesday morning, the wind was from the north, the weather was clear with sunshine. We rode against the high ascending mountain range until midday, when we were on top of the Dlecke Fauck Onnij. We lodged here; there is a large standing pool. We rode through an uneven, stony, difficult path downward. It began to snow. We arrived in the evening in the city of Oudauhxee, having ridden eight miles.

The 3rd, Thursday, the wind was from the north-east with clear, cold weather. I know not [what happened] in a meadow, and we transported the pack horses with bridges over which we came through ice. We lodged in Fonsesau, a place in the evening. We arrived in the evening in the Elecke Cammangaulle, having ridden thirteen miles.

The 4th, Friday morning, the wind and weather were as before. A Japanese servant was sent to inform the lord Jan Fixando, our companion, and to arrange the lodging. I requested to speak with the lord and to deliver my cargo and letters, but this was not possible. After we had eaten something, we walked in the courtyard, examined the dwelling and his horses. I delivered the letter from His Excellency to the lord president, [explaining] that we had come with the greatest haste in this great cold in order to demand the release of the unfortunate Mr. Nuijts. I requested His Excellency to use his influence, and to make the promise a reality through action. Sunday morning, the wind was from the south with cold, sunny weather. First thing, His Imperial Majesty wished to visit the pagoda at Snrangau. January: In the name of the Lord, 1636: In the Emperor's city of Gedo in Japan: also the lord van Fixando and the councilors, and my companion was advised. Two [of them] had my black servant fetched, so that to the lady's amusement he appeared and was presented with a silk robe. [We] remained waiting for the summons.

The 7th, Monday morning, the wind was from the north with weather as before. The secretary Seroshedon of the lord came on horseback to our lodging and let it be known that I should go with him to the castle at the house of the lord Tackemosamma. We were carried there in a Noximom [a type of sedan chair] with carriers. We waited around one and a half hours. There were three times as many people, and the aforementioned councilor with great attendance and his retinue and children came to visit us. The aforementioned Seroskedon spoke the word. He answered politely and kindly how his month had now passed. He advised us to present a short Request in three days at the house of the councilor Sannike Samma, who would then preside. We promised to induce the same lord and to undertake all good offices toward a speedy dispatch. With that we departed to our lodging. The aforementioned secretary reported the same to the lord van Fixando, so that the request would be formulated and made ready by the limited day.

He declared that he had been in the castle at the house of the councilor Sannick Samma, where he had first heard our Request. The aforementioned lord had taken it into consideration.

The 12th, Saturday morning, the wind was as before with a topsail breeze, sunny weather. We understood through the interpreter that the lord Jan Firando had ridden out that day to advance the matter, and His Majesty had gone hunting. The ambassador of our lord Kakeseijmon came to visit me, also gave good hope for the outcome of the matter.

Our interpreter reported that the lord van Fixando had ridden to the castle to advance our matter with the lord councilors. text_translated_detailed: Per the General Comptoir [expanded: General Accounting Office] on Batavia to the following ƒ 101217/11/7/— For so much as the debts listed below, and sent cash payments, as well as other accounts. To the Lord of Firando [Hirado]: Your Excellency's very pleasant letter of the 28th day of the 12th month to the lord president, was received by us through the chief merchant Hagenaer on the water between Osaka and Firando, very well, from which Your Excellency's good disposition we have understood with pleasure, wishing that the same may succeed unchangingly. On the other hand, it has again grieved us to see how the aforementioned Hagenaer, fruitlessly without having accomplished anything, was sent back again and the settlement of the governor's affairs has been postponed once more. We shall not doubt but firmly hope that they will finally now with our personal appearance there be obtained through Your Excellency's help and favor. We arrived well with the gifts on the 25th day of the first month in Osaka, and we hasten ourselves so much to appear before Your Excellency as is in any way possible, which, if the weather permits, will happen around the 11th or 12th day of the 2nd month. The Honorable Captain Couckebacker departed on the 9th day of the first month, after whose departure and the sending off of all the ships, we have also waited somewhat to come above, of all which arriving there Your Excellency will receive instruction and satisfaction. On the day of the 1st month, being from François Garon in Dutch style 7th March 1636: Natsura Fisenoca misame Jan Firando: Your Excellency's valued letter dated the 1st day of the 5th month was received by us on the 3rd day of the 6th month with great joy, from which with a singular gladness we have seen the great favor and the distinguished honor that his Imperial Majesty through Your Excellency's doing and help has been pleased to show to us and the governor, which gift of 200:

text_translated_detailed:
Tackimon samma. François Gazon. To the most principal Regents of the Kingdom:

We send Your Excellencies this Express messenger principally to thank Your Excellencies in a friendly manner, that our servant Itsiseijmon has been so helpful in the past year in permitting us to purchase camphor, such that we have obtained satisfaction of our request in part according to our wishes. This expression of thanks should properly have taken place earlier, which we acknowledge, and it would also have occurred had our journey to Edo to pay reverence to His Imperial Majesty not prevented it. For this reason we request that the negligence be taken in good part. This year we hope again to obtain a good quantity of camphor. We therefore request respectfully that Your Excellencies be pleased to grant us the same, for which we shall remain grateful if this may come to pass. The circumstances shall be conveyed to Your Excellencies orally by our servant. Should Your Excellencies require anything within our power, please command us and we shall always be found in Your Excellencies' service. As a token of this letter we send Your Excellencies these small presents, namely: Nigzo Gangano Camij samma, 1 piece of fine cotton and 1 piece of double silk. Hen Gauwa Camij, C. t hion gin samma, 1 piece of fine cotton and 1 piece of double silk. Chimaes daijnsio samma, 1 piece of double silk. For the General Comptoir in Batavia the following amount: ƒ 101,217/11/7 [modern equivalent: Dutch guilders, shillings, and pence] for the debts listed below and remitted funds, as well as other accounts. We request and moreover ask that Your Excellencies receive this gift with good heart. 720 Cangom Camij samma. On the 5th month, 5th day, according to Dutch style the 5th of August in the year 1636. To Cauwa Canij Chionginsamma. D hiemaes daijn sio samma. Signed: François Caron. To the Lord of Firando.

Your Excellency's agreeable letter dated the 5th month, 9th day we have indeed received, for which the Express messenger thanks you most respectfully. All that Your Excellency has charged us with therein, as well as what we have understood verbally from the queamosqued [uncertain: possibly a title or official], we shall obey in all respects and on our part follow the command of the high authority. text_translated_detailed: gifts for His Majesty, as well as other great lords in Japan, not equally but according to different occasions and opportunities to be used. Extraordinarily fine engraved rider's armor, shot-proof, yet not too heavy, and that burnished. Similar light armor. Field cannons, long and light of new invention, shooting 9, 10, 11, or 12 pound [modern equivalent: approximately 4-5.4 kg] iron balls with their ramparts and further accessories. Leather pieces, similar to those used by the Majesty of Sweden in the army, shooting the largest balls, as before with their accessories. One very large, fine, heavy clock with its wheels to make it chime. Large tapestries or made canopies with trees, gardens, and all manner of water and land birds therein, of the largest, heaviest English make. Muskets from which one can fire several shots from one barrel, and that one after another shoots along with it. Some very fine, delicate glass frames that are painted with four small ships, warfare and landscapes. Some very fine crystalline nose spectacles set in gold and silver. Two extraordinary far-seeing telescopes with gold tubes, very fine and elegantly enameled, and such rare goods, more that are unknown to us, as their Honors shall be pleased to send hither. All manner of instruments and tools to make various and such fireworks as are presently used in the Netherlands at the siege of cities, whereby then a master or another who understands himself thoroughly therein should be sent hither, which at the Comptoir [expanded: trading post] Firando this present November 28th, 1636: Bouckebacker 8686

In purchase: Raw white silk cost per the other [unit], 489 guilders. The first sorting cost per the other [unit]. The second sorting cost per the other [unit]. Quinamsche silk cost per the other [unit], 332 guilders. Red Gielams at 18 months per piece. White Gielams at 15 months per piece. Velvet costs per the other [unit], 11 guilders 12 stuivers. Pelinghs, namely double width figured pieces at 5 Rixdollars [modern equivalent: approximately 2.5 guilders] per piece; double pieces somewhat narrower at 5 and 4¾ Rixdollars per piece; double pieces still somewhat narrower at 4¼ and 4½ Rixdollars per piece. Tajouansche harterells, heads at 13 stuivers per hundred.

text_translated_detailed: and Esteemed Lord General Antonio van Diemen [Antonio van Diemen: Dutch VOC Governor-General], Esteemed Valiant, Wise, Prudent and most Discreet Lord. Your Esteemed Missive of the 29th of December last by the ship the Galeas [galeas: a type of ship], as well as of the 19th of January with the Yacht Texel, came to us on the 21st of February by the Galeas, and on the 3rd of March with the Yacht Texel successively. Upon which we, due to the shortness of time according to our governance, could not answer. But we shall defer the same until the next dispatch. Upon which request Your Esteemed [person] has been pleased to take kindly, since it is not through negligence but through lack of time that it occurred. The cargoes sent to us, after receipt thereof, we have had loaded for the Moluccas and delivered to the general goods. The Galeas, on the return journey, ran aground in the Strait of Banten, so that we were forced to come off from there again, throwing some rice overboard, on account of which from the 46 loads of rice sent, 8 came short. Likewise 2 barrels of arrack [arrack: a type of alcohol] which we found completely empty. In the case with fabrics, there is also missing one roll of cloves [chioel: cloves]; the invoice says 5, but only 4 were found. And from the 40 loads of rice from the Yacht Texel, 6½ loads, so that in place of the 86 loads sent to us, we received only 72. Your Esteemed [person] has been pleased to write to us in the Missive of the 29th of December by the Galeas, that we, as well here as Your Esteemed there, should have understood that it was not intended to send any relief to the treacherous Rampsia [Rampsia: likely a local ruler], nor to allow any force of ships or people to come at his request. On account of which Your Esteemed and the Honored Council of India there seem to have some displeasure. However, the gentlemen may trust that our request or instance for any relief or aid was not

text_translated_detailed: The Council found it good to send the ships Thoolen and Texel, which was still unloaded, immediately, with orders to join up with the galley, so that we might understand whether we could still achieve something advantageous against the enemy. However, the ships were indeed sent toward the enemy, but nothing was accomplished, since the enemy's ships were rowed forward and brought inside by the galley and the multitude of Tidorese Correcorre [indigenous war vessels]. If our ships had come to us ten to fourteen days before the enemy, and had been sent to sea to cruise near Malcander, we trust that we would have accomplished something advantageous against the enemy there, but the time has now been too short and our relief came too late, which grieves us. The Spanish force consists of two ships, one mounted with forty-six metal cannons and the other with thirty, the third being a yacht with ten cannons with an Origantijn [type of vessel] to which was attached the galley that ordinarily remains in Moluco, manned besides the ordinary boat crew, and the galley with five companies of Spaniards, strong—three hundred men. Besides this, two more companies of Pampangers, each strong one hundred twenty-five men; this is their force that they have now brought from Manila with these ships. On the fourteenth of March we received a deserter, a slave, who informed us that with these five companies of Spaniards over fifty captains and ensigns Reformado [reformed officers] had come, and that it had been said there for some time that with this relief that had come, the Moluco would now be completely freed from the Hollanders. Many and various persons were sent by the Old King of Tydoor to learn everything, and the news came in all respects in agreement. King Hampsia sent a kiepe lamma [indigenous messenger/envoy] to Tydoor to learn everything and to report back to us upon his return.

text_translated_detailed: Over fifty captains and ensigns Reformado had come, and it had been said there for some time that with this relief that had come, the Moluco would now be completely freed from the Hollanders. Fearing being attacked over this, the aforementioned Gougoe threw himself overboard into his Correcorre and departed hastily toward land, taking refuge with King Gorentalij.

But no answer was given to us on this matter. Your Excellency also burdens us with the making of a Runduer [fortification] on Tabalola to proceed with, whether with or against the will of the King and Macqianese, recommending to us to go speedily about it, as was done by the Esteemed President Ottens on Pouant in such a short time. My Lord, please trust us that we shall have everything in readiness as was the case at that time when Ponatti began to be built, that we shall advance the work as loyally as any other, but it shall be somewhat different to begin this building on Tabalola than it was on Pouatti aforesaid. It will not be able to proceed so conveniently there, nor shall we have a Sengadia of Grofficqua who will help us fetch the stone for the work. Also, the distance will not be so short between Tabalola and Grofficqia to be able to bring all materials of lime and wood and otherwise. Your Excellency is pleased to consider if the Tarnatae here will be against us in this, and the Tidorese will pass on our vessel as before, what opportunity we shall have to accommodate ourselves. I have found in the shipping of the cloves the previous year what trouble we had and what costs had to be incurred for the Company before we could bring 90 bahars [modern equivalent: approximately 4,500 kg] of cloves from Tabalola to Grofficqua. text_translated_detailed: That which by the church council of the city Batavia has been provided to the wife of Lieutenant Philips Cranevelt by loan, of which resolution is requested. It is so that the mentioned Lieutenant Cranevelt in the month of November in the year 1635 of this world has passed away and has by testament disposed of all his remaining goods to various persons, only bequeathing to Madalena Redrigo 200 Rixdollars [modern equivalent: a substantial sum in 17th-century currency] of eight reals each, not recognizing her as his wife. The reasons for this, Your Excellency there knows better than we do. However, notwithstanding this, we have not let the legacies be received, but have held everything together to await your order thereupon. The testament as well as the inventory of that which said Lieutenant has cleared away and left behind with his death shall come to Your Excellency with the first ships departing from here, upon which we shall await your decision.

text_translated_detailed: To the Noble General Antonio van Diemen [Antonio van Diemen], Noble, Valiant, Wise, Provident, and most Discreet Sir — Our letter to Your Excellency is from the 20th of March concerning Amboina, by which Your Excellency shall well have understood the safe arrival of ships: the galeas [galley] on the 21st of February and the Texel on the 3rd of March past, which we trust shall have come into Your Excellency's hands before the receipt of this, of which a copy is enclosed herewith. Your Excellency shall thereby have observed what has transpired in the quarters of Molucco [Moluccas], since our arrival there. Since then, on the 17th of April, there arrived safely to us in Molucco from Amboina the yachts Tergoes and Zeeburch [Seaburg], together with Your Excellency's esteemed letter of the 19th of February, by which from Batavia there were sent to us 1700 bales of Japanese rice, and 300 from Amboina, making together 2000 bales, which we have charged to Molucco according to the invoice, and have had the General account for it. Except that with the rice from the galeas eight and from the Texel 6½ lasts [modern equivalent: approximately 8-10 tons per last] come up short, making together 14½ lasts, which is considerable for the sparse amount sent to us at this time. With the cargo that came to us with the yacht Tergoes, there is also missing, as likewise appears from the invoice and bill of lading, a case with silk fabrics numbered 113, which we have not received. We have spoken to the skipper and merchant about this, who say that said case they have not received, nor was it in the ship, as Your Excellency shall be able to observe from the attached document. From our previous letter as well as a copy of the Resolution, Your Excellency shall have understood what reasons moved us to detain the ships the galeas and Texel and not to send them to Amboina according to Your Excellency's order, which we have also advised to the Governor and the Council in Amboina by express prau [a type of sailing vessel].

This request of his seems to be founded partly on reasons, but we shall submit our opinion on this under Your Honored's wise judgment. As far as we have been able to see and understand, this Batsjan is very rich in cloves, which are mostly obtained from the Tidorese, and if this request is denied to the King, it is to be feared that no cloves will come to us but all will go to the Tidorese and Spanish. It is true that the Honored Company at this time has little concern for this circumstance, but then we would have to allow the same to be carried to the Spanish, which would not be at all tolerable for us. As far as concerns the power of this King of Batsjan, it is very small; we cannot trust that if all his people were brought together that it would amount to more than 300 men, and as far as concerns the laborers who bear the name of Christians and fall under our obedience, they are strong in general with women, children and slaves, about 120 souls, of which about 50 are men, which are mostly rogues and scoundrels that can be found in any quarters, leaning much more toward Mohammedanism than toward us. What good the Company can expect from this, please Your Honored consider. As soon as we had completed our business on Batsjan, we departed from there toward Macquan [Makian], and having arrived there, we had the begun fort continue to be raised, and while we were occupied with this, all the chief leaders of Macqian appeared before us to come speak with us about the delivery of cloves, as there daily many troubles and disputes arose over the weighing of them, since very dirty and damp cloves were brought to the trading posts, against which our merchants objected, telling them that they had received them to accept cloves but no dirt or filth, they complained about us that we demanded from them what no governors before us had imposed upon them, and that the cloves had never been brought to the trading posts so pure as now, and that we were still not satisfied with it, whereupon they now brought with them three sorts of rings of cloves, from which they requested that we choose one, after which they would then regulate all their cloves to bring them so, the first sorting presented to us was found to be so impure that half of it was mostly stems, husks and filth, these they said should be paid for at 50 Rixdollars [modern equivalent: Dutch currency] per bahar [modern equivalent: unit of weight, approximately 150-180 kg], the other sorting was not or scarcely better, must be paid for at 60 Rixdollars, and the third sorting was pure just as they should be delivered, these they said must be paid for at no less than 100 Rixdollars, and so if we desired to have cloves we must regulate ourselves accordingly, since they had decided to deal no otherwise, wanting our resolution on this, saying also that they were tired of all the quarrels that daily arose over the delivery of cloves, from which disputes they desired to be relieved —

text_translated_detailed: SERVICE ACCOUNT. To the Esteemed Lord General van Dirmen [uncertain: possibly "van Diermen"] at Antonio Lolh, Manhafte, Wi: wijst [uncertain: unclear abbreviation] 1712 Foresight in this discretion E=tOnsen Tongsten to Your Esteemed [abbreviated: Your Esteemed]. My Lord, In date the eleventh of June in the year 1636, per the yacht Ter Goes [normalized version: "The Goes"], of which a copy is enclosed herewith, we hope that the same, together with the return shipment of cloves that was sent, will have arrived before the receipt of this letter. Your Esteemed in safety, which shall have arrived, this goes per the yacht Zeeburch [normalized version: "Seaburg"], with which Your Esteemed are being sent 172133 pounds [modern equivalent: approximately 78,000 kilograms] of pure cloves, costing with the duties and underweight f 38858, 16, 4. May God Almighty be pleased to let this and the previous shipment arrive safely at the proper time. Here in Molucco [normalized version: Moluccas] there still remain over Bamoffel cloves: 37 [uncertain: possibly a measure or quantity designation] Bhaeren [uncertain: unclear term], which could not be loaded due to the smallness of this and the previous yacht. Since our most recent letter, nothing extraordinary has occurred here in Molucco, but everything remains and continues in the previous terms with the Ternataens [normalized version: people of Ternate]. It continues in peace with the Tidorees [normalized version: people of Tidore], though it appears that he is taking some action of hostility against the Spaniard, but we cannot determine that he is serious about it. Nevertheless, the Spaniard does him all the damage that is possible for him. It is true that many and various garrisons of the Ternataens are positioned against him, but nothing good is ever accomplished thereby, so that the powder and lead of the Company are merely wasted, which wearies us. The subjects of the Tidorees, such as those of Mauar and other places, were about a month ago near Gammacnorra on the coast of Mooro with their vessels, and captured about 168 persons from the Ternataen people from there. We would have liked to speak with King Hampsia in this opportunity to understand whether one could not bring him, through this and many other damages that the Company was suffering daily, to turn his weapons against them, but however many times and often we had him summoned through our interpreters, he would not appear before us, always excusing himself under one pretext or another.

text_translated_detailed: The new Gougoe [uncertain: possibly a title or rank] Eitchil Moussa, together with three other Colano Noffagnaris [uncertain: possibly titles or names], were sent by the King two or three times to us, with which we had many and various reasons regarding the long absence of the King, as well as what reasons for discontent there were, that all the great ones, namely Soasieras and sengadjas, held the Gougoe so strangely and aversely. In answer to this, the Gougoe said that the King was ashamed to appear before us, and that for reasons, he had made us real and great promises to undertake the war against the Tidorees, and that upon all his promises, nothing had followed thus far, saying this alone was the reason that held the King back from coming to us. With the Colano Noffagnaris we had many reasons about this matter as well, namely regarding this aversion, both on their part and on the King's part, which they answered us by saying that since the killing of sengadja of Gammacnorra and his son, as well as the deposition of the sengadja of Guofficqia, a great fear had come upon them, seeing that if anyone of theirs sought the company of Dutchmen somewhat more than the King approved, they would be held suspect and hated, whereby they could expect nothing else than death, or at least their ruin and destruction, saying this alone was the cause that they showed themselves so strangely and aversely to us.

However, we cannot lose sight of the fact that little will come of this, and that this is merely put forward by Hampsia to make us feel that everything is meant rightly by him. Daily experience teaches us that all his acts and proceedings are based on falsehood and deception, and that he seeks nothing but the Company's damage and ruin. He said furthermore that he recommended to us the speed of our journey, so that before the departure of Zeeburch the matter could be brought so far that we could write to Your Excellency and the Lords Council of India that the war against the Tidorese had now come to him, and was being pursued with earnestness and force, so that his letter might once be believed by Your Excellency and the Lords Council of India. The words and promises were indeed good, but in the execution of these promises we are very much in doubt. — In these reasons being so, we meanwhile also put before him his past falsehoods, and how often he had deceived us with lies. But to this we received no answer, except that one should not think of the past anymore, but that one should have good trust in one another, insofar as it concerned him. He now wanted to show that everything was meant rightly by him, requesting that we have no ill feeling or mistrust of his person, and that everything would be well, saying furthermore that as soon as we had departed, he would send all the Gougoe [uncertain: ethnic/regional designation] to Machan [place name], to gather all the power from there with others. He wanted to go in person himself to Gilolo [place name] to prepare everything there for the war as well, so that for our Company everything would be ready. We told him that this matter was already being made too public, and that the Tidorese would without doubt get knowledge of it and arm themselves against it. To which our answer was, even if the Tidorese knew everything, he would nevertheless proceed with his planned work and carry it out. — With this the King took his leave, and we went aboard and continued our journey to Batsjan, where having arrived we found everything concerning the Company's state and condition in reasonable order. 726 Brief Account Extracted from the Daily Register kept in Moluco from the 16th of August in the year 1635 until the 1st of June following—

After the departure of the Esteemed President Ottens, we have daily pressed the King of Ternate [Ternaten], so that according to his promises, with the beginning of the war against the Spaniard and Tidorese, he would proceed further. However, he wished to continue disregarding the good admonitions and warnings which we had previously given him, without deceiving us any longer with idle promises through pretense and lies, so that the ruin of his realm would not be further advanced. Nevertheless, this worked on the 27th of August last past, when we sent the interpreter again to the King, with a similar reminder of his obligatory duty, and at the same time we told him that the Esteemed Company's affairs required our beloved son on Makian [Macian]. Following this, we had resolved to send a ship, the Thoolen, in that direction, to which His Majesty answered us that the slow progress of the beginning of the war troubled him, and that this arose from the long delay of the praus and people that had to come from the opposite coast, which had already been expected here for two days, promising that as soon as they arrived, he would eagerly seize the war by the hand. Over and above this, he earnestly and urgently requested that we would arrange such order with the respective heads here at our departure, that according to the promise made upon the navigation of the Esteemed President Ottens toward Batavia, Raconi [uncertain: possibly a place name] with our Christian people (the war beginning) would be occupied and could be maintained. Accordingly, on the 30th following, having embarked in the aforementioned Thoolen, on the 3rd of September we arrived safely at the roadstead before Ouofficqia [uncertain: place name]. Whereupon it should be very astonishing to them that all the services of our lords and masters to the realm of Ternate, with so many treasures and Dutch blood, were now being rewarded with mistrust, and that those whom their Excellencies had helped to rise, made great, and brought into a flourishing state, were now attempting to erect forts against them, consequently for love nor for fear would we not permit the erection of the work, but would prevent and forestall it with all the means that God had granted us. Two days thereafter we received news from Macgian that 2 of our ships had been seen there, after which news the authorities sent the Comi again above, who presented to us that the King had recounted all that we had recently declared against them in the meeting, likewise that in the most recent meeting it had been decided, as we noticed and found, just as we had, in forbidding the fortress (they suspected and could well perceive that the erection would be entirely harmful and disadvantageous for our fort), therefore it should be left undone, and furthermore the begun work would be allowed to fall into ruin. Thereupon this should be agreeable to us, and we recommended to them further, that we would never make any unreasonable proposals to them, but would request that which is right and just, for we would regulate ourselves accordingly, furthermore, recounting at length and in detail the affronts shown to us by them on Macgian here and elsewhere, together with many other circumstances besides. text_original: 3S PREAIET Op donderdach desen xxiii1=en Januarij A„o 1636 alsoo op xxii=en der Iegenwoordighe Maent van Ianuarij den Coninck Hampsia van Tarnaten, den hoecom limorij aen d' E: Heer Jan Broeckum Raedt Dan Indja, Goeverneur ende directeur over de Molucos. ende den Raet: als gecommitteerde heeft gesonden, omme zijne E: ende hare achtbaerheijden int breede vooren te dragen, ende te verclaeren, de groote ende Menichvuldige clachten (:der Inwoonderen vant Eijlandt Macqian) die dagelijcx voor zijne Maijs„t met mennichten quamen, over de quade bejegenninge als anders, die hun door den oppercoopman Sr„ Nicolaes Cloedt wierden aengedaen, gelijck zijne voorsz. Maijs„ op gisteren noch sekeren Brieff ten dien Eijnde becomen hadt, welcken onder andere jnhoude, dat d'overicheijt van t gantsche Eijlandt gesamentlijk versochten, ende Insisteerde, zijne Maijs„t tot lichtingh der gemelte oppercoopman, ende dat met een ander persoon versien mochten werden, bij den Heer Gouverneur harent wegen wilde Intercideeren, dienvolgende zijn Maijs„t niet hadde connen naerlaeten, zulcx te doen, ten eijnde bij zijne E. daer op geleth ende naer behooren gedisponneert werden mochte, ende naer dien wel gemelte Heer Gouverneur gansch ernstich versocht, lictuire ende translaet vanden Brieff te mogen hebben, op dat met fondament naer bevindingh mochte werden gehandelt, is heeden wesende xxiiii=m Januarij. voorsz Hoecom Limori als gedeputeerde van zijne Maijst van Tarnaten ongemelte brieff met hem bracht :) bij den Heere Gouvernende den Raedt, Colegialiter vergadert zijnde, weder Audientie vergunt, die wt last ende bevel zijnes Conincx andermael proponneerde ende Claechde, als vooren over gemelte oppercoopman, van t Eijlandt Macqians proceduiren, Onder expresse protestatie, van in toe comende onschuldich te willen wesen, soo door des selfs continuatie ende voortganck zijner regieringie, aldaer eenighe onheijlen quamen te ontstaen, alsoo zijne E. ende den Raedt, daer van nu genouchsaem hadde gewaerschouwt, naert welcke de Missive in volle vergaderingh bij den Hoccom
text_translated_detailed: 3S PREAIET On Thursday the twenty-third of January in the year 1636, as on the twenty-second of the present month of January the King Hampsia of Ternate, the reason Limori to the Esteemed Lord Jan Broeckum Councillor in India, Governor and director over the Moluccas, and the Council: as commissioned has sent, in order to his Excellency and their worships in broad manner to present, and to declare, the great and manifold complaints (of the inhabitants of the island of Macqian) which daily came before his Majesty in multitudes, over the bad treatment as otherwise, which were done to them by the chief merchant Sir Nicholas Cloedt, as his aforesaid Majesty yesterday still received a certain Letter to that end, which among other contents, that the authorities of the whole island together requested, and insisted, his Majesty to the removal of the mentioned chief merchant, and that with another person be provided, by the Lord Governor on their behalf would intercede, accordingly his Majesty could not have failed to do such, to the end that by his Excellency thereupon be laid and after proper be disposed, and after which the mentioned Lord Governor very earnestly requested, copy and translation of the Letter to be able to have, so that with foundation after finding could be handled, is today being the twenty-fourth of January aforesaid, the Hoecom Limori as deputy of his Majesty of Ternate brought the mentioned letter with him :) by the Lord Governor and the Council, collegially gathered being, again audience granted, who by order and command of his King again proposed and complained, as before over the mentioned chief merchant, of the island of Macqian's proceeding, Under express protestation, of in coming to be innocent, so through the same's continuation and progress of his governance, there any misfortunes came to arise, as his Excellency and the Council, thereof now sufficiently had been warned, after which the Missive in full gathering by the Hoecom

text_translated_detailed: collegially gathered being, again audience granted, who by order and command of his King again proposed and complained, as before over the mentioned chief merchant, of the island of Macqian's proceeding, Under express protestation, of in coming to be innocent, so through the same's continuation and progress of his governance, there any misfortunes came to arise, as his Excellency and the Council, thereof now sufficiently had been warned, after which the Missive in full gathering by the Hoecom was read, and by the Interpreter Alonso Cardanoso translated being in substance into the Dutch language as follows: Most Mighty King, your subjects, we three Sengadjas and all the Chimelahas of the island of Macqian, beseech your Majesty that it please you to speak to the Lord Governor, and to say, if his Excellency takes any regard for the Company's state, means and trade here on the island, that he please to remove the merchant of Onofficqua and place another in his place, for he has made the weight of the daetche [uncertain: possibly a local measure or scale] heavier and sells the goods to us at a higher price than the list brings, and desires to receive no nails otherwise than such that are excessively dry, three quarters of the quantity completely pure, and the further fourth part, with clear stalks mixed are, we bring our nails to the purchase, but he does not desire to receive them, the daetche of Tabalola is also made heavier in the weight, such that we people all together, have intended and resolved, no nails to the Comptoirs at Onofficqua and Tabalola shall deliver, but request to your Majesty that it please you to make known to the Lord Governor that we all our nails at Taffascho (where the weight is correct) may weigh, and deliver, if the Lord Governor, the merchant of Onofficqua will not remove, and from that any misfortunes came to arise,

text_original: 3R225 A REAEN Verclaeringe van eenen Bastiaen leeuwa geboortich van Manilha, die dit Iaer met het spaens secours van daer nu jn Moluco gecomen was ende van Gammalamma bij ons op Maleijen overgecomen, desen Persoon hadde twee Jaren aenden anderen met de schepen van Manilra In Noda Spangien ofte aguapulcque geweest Desen Bastiaen Leeuwa, hebben bij ons ontboden, ende hem naer alle gelegentheijt vande Reijsen wt Manilha naer Noda Spangien Ondervraecht, Eerstelijk in wat maent, dese schepen wt Manilha haer reijse beginnen, ende hoe lange zij op de vooijagie zijn al eer jn aguapulcque comen, ten anderen als dese schepen het silver in Nova spangien hebben jngenomen, om wat tijt de selve wederom van daer Naer Manisha Vertrecken, ende hoe lange op de selve reijse zijn, al eer daer comen te arriveeren oock wat quantiteijt silver ofte Realen van achten rij„— mede brengen, Seijt dat de schepen, die wt Manilha Vertrecken, naer Nol a spangien ofte aguapulcque, gaen t' zeijl jnde maent van Iulij, tussschen den 10=en ende 25=en, ende brengen toe aleer jn Nova Spangien comen„ 5„ maenden 25 dagen, Oock Twel: 6: maenden, ende meer, naer dat de schepen wel bezeijlt zijn Ende als het silver In Aguapulque hebben in genomen scheijden van daer jnde Maent van Maert tusschen den 5=e ende den 15=en sonder langer te tarderen, zijnde dan onder wech aleer de Eijlanden ladronis passeeren tussschen de 40: ende 50: dagen, altemet 42: 3: 4„ ende 45 dagen maer ten langhsten niet boven de 50 Ende dan voorts van de Ladronis tot de Cabo del spirito sancto ofte den Bockaderen brengen toe, 20„ 21„ ofte „22„ dagen, soo dat altijt inde Maent Maijus den Embocadere passseren ofte door comen, soo dat het arivement der schepen, wt Nova spangien in Manilha altijt is omtrent S„t Jan, altemet
text_translated_detailed: 3R225 A STATEMENT Clarification from a certain Bastiaen Leeuwa, born in Manila, who came this year with the Spanish reinforcements from there and is now in the Moluccas and came over to us at Gammalamma on the Malay coast. This person had spent two years consecutively with the ships from Manila in Nueva España or Acapulco. We summoned this Bastiaen Leeuwa and interrogated him regarding all the circumstances of the voyages from Manila to Nueva España, first of all in what month these ships depart from Manila and how long they are at sea before arriving in Acapulco, secondly when these ships have taken on silver in Nueva España, after what time they depart again from there for Manila and how long they are at sea before arriving there, and also what quantity of silver or reales of eight they bring with them. He says that the ships which depart from Manila for Nueva España or Acapulco set sail in the month of July, between the 10th and 25th, and take five months and 25 days before arriving in Nueva España, or also twelve, six months, and more, depending on how well the ships are sailed. And when they have taken on the silver in Acapulco, they depart from there in the month of March between the 5th and 15th without delaying any longer, being then underway before passing the Ladrone Islands [Mariana Islands] between 40 and 50 days, at times 42, 3/4, and 45 days, but at the longest not more than 50. And then from the Ladrones to Cape del Espíritu Santo or the Bocadera [entrance to Manila Bay], they take 20, 21, or 22 days, so that they always pass through the entrance in the month of May, so that the arrival of the ships from Nueva España in Manila is always around Saint John's Day [June 24], at times

He says that when the ships arrive around Saint John's Day, they spend most of that time in the strait of Manila, as they are always tormented there by silt and opposing currents. In the previous year of 1635, the same Bastiaen Leeuwa says that with these two ships which are now in the Moluccas, he came from Acapulco to Manila, and that 10 days after Saint John's Day, which was the 3rd of July, they anchored before Cavite, which he said was very smooth sailing, and that people in Manila were already fearful that the ships had encountered some misfortune. As for the quantity of silver or reales of eight that came with the ships, he said this was unknown to him, as it was not told to them but kept hidden. text_translated_detailed: kept hidden. We further asked him how these ships were armed and with how many men they were provided. He said that when he came the previous year from Nueva España with these 2 ships, the Admiral was named Nuestra Señora de Concepción, armed with 36 metal cannons, and the Vice Admiral with 30, having between them over 400 soldiers, besides passengers and their ship's crew, and that the ships which came from Nueva España were always well armed and provided with men. It is to be trusted that if our ships had encountered these two ships the previous year, there would not have been much advantage to be gained, so that, according to our opinion, Your Reverend Excellency and the Gentlemen Councillors of India in Batavia should resolve to undertake this exploit against the Acapulco silver ships again, for which at least four well-armed ships should be employed. We trust that if this design is carried out, it will eventually succeed, and God Almighty will let them fall into our hands at last. This is as much as we have been able to learn about these Acapulco silver ships. We have interrogated the person Bastiaen Leeuwa here on five different occasions, each 3 or 4 days apart from one another, but he always persisted in his given statement without our finding any change in it in any manner whatsoever.
